title: BSAA Star Ariel disappearance
summary: BSAA Star Ariel departed Bermuda on January 17, 1949, with 20 aboard bound for Kingston, Jamaica. The pilot reported good visibility at 18,000 feet and a course change to communications frequency 6523 kc/s at 09:42. No further messages were received. Despite extensive search over 55,000 square miles no wreckage was found. The cause of loss remains unknown, though communication problems and possible frequency change issues were investigated.

title: 1949 Exhall mid-air collision
summary: On 19 February 1949, a British European Airways Douglas DC-3 collided with a Royal Air Force Avro Anson T21 near Exhall, Coventry. The Dakota was en route from Northolt to Glasgow with a crew of four and six passengers. The Avro was on a training flight from RAF Middleton St. George. At approximately 10:00, in clear weather at 4,500 feet, the Avro struck the Dakota at the root of the right wing. Both aircraft were destroyed with no survivors.
probable_cause: The investigation concluded that the crew of neither aircraft saw each other, possibly due to glare from the sun, and blamed the accident on a failure of both captains to keep a proper look-out for other aircraft.

title: 1949 Queensland Airlines Lockheed Lodestar crash
summary: The aircraft took off at 11:15 am but before reaching 300 feet altitude it pitched nose-up into a near-vertical attitude after undercarriage retraction. The aircraft stalled and crashed onto its belly into a swamp beyond the airstrip. Investigation revealed the aircraft was loaded with its centre of gravity behind the rear limit due to errors in the load chart that did not account for undercarriage retraction. Additionally, the elevator trim tab was found set for landing instead of takeoff.
probable_cause: The aircraft was loaded with its centre of gravity behind the rear limit of 39% MAC, and the elevator trim tab was not set for takeoff, making the aircraft uncontrollable.

title: Superga air disaster
summary: A Fiat G.212 airliner carrying the entire Torino football team on final approach to Turin in poor weather crashed into the retaining wall at the Basilica of Superga. The crew descended below safe altitude in mountainous terrain with the altimeter possibly locked at an incorrect reading, and strong crosswinds may have caused drift from the intended approach path.
probable_cause: The aircraft either suffered drift from strong left crosswinds or the altimeter malfunctioned and locked at 2000 m, leading the pilots to believe they were at a higher altitude than they actually were, resulting in controlled flight into the hill.

The plane crashed into the back of the embankment of the Basilica of Superga.

title: 1949 Strato-Freight Curtiss C-46A crash

location.name: Atlantic Ocean west of San Juan

summary: The C-46D crashed into the Atlantic Ocean approximately one minute after takeoff from San Juan. The right engine failed, and investigation determined the aircraft had been loaded 3,709 pounds over maximum weight at 48,709 pounds. Improper maintenance included installation of thirteen AC-LS-87 spark plugs not approved for the Pratt and Whitney engines, and the ignition switch was set to fire only rear spark plugs. The aircraft could not maintain altitude on one engine at its overloaded weight.
probable_cause: The loss of power of the right engine before the aircraft attained the optimum single engine climb speed, together with the overloaded condition of the aircraft, resulted in it losing altitude and settling into the sea.

title: 1949 MacRobertson Miller Aviation DC-3 crash
summary: The DC-3 Fitzroy took off from Perth Airport at 2:14 am on 2 July 1949 in driving rain with 10 miles visibility. The aircraft climbed unusually quickly to about 500 feet then rolled and spiraled vertically to the ground. Investigation found the aircraft had stalled and the pilots were unable to regain control. Weight and balance issues were suspected as the aircraft may have been loaded with excess cargo in the rear baggage locker.
probable_cause: aircraft stalled during initial climb; pilots unable to regain control; weight and balance near or beyond limits

title: Standard Air Lines 897R
summary: Flight 897R was on an ILS approach to Burbank when it descended below the minimum altitude in patchy fog. The right wing tip struck a hillside at 1,890 feet and the aircraft bounced 300 feet before crashing in Chatsworth, 430 feet below the Santa Susana Pass crest. The CAB determined the accident was caused solely by the pilot voluntarily descending below the prescribed minimum altitude.

title: 1949 Manchester BEA Douglas DC-3 accident
summary: A British European Airways Douglas DC-3 crashed on Saddleworth Moor in the Pennines while approaching Manchester Airport. After an hour of flight from Belfast, the aircraft struck a mist-covered hill near Chew Valley, approximately 20 feet from the summit while flying at 1,350 feet. The investigation attributed the accident to navigation error, incorrect approach procedure, and failure to check aircraft position accurately before descent. Twenty-four of 32 occupants died.

title: 1949 Air France Lockheed Constellation crash
summary: Air France Flight 009, a Lockheed L-749A Constellation, crashed into a ridge between Pico da Vara and Pico Redondo on São Miguel Island in the Azores on 28 October 1949 while attempting to land at Santa Maria Airport. The pilot reported being at 3000 feet with the airport in sight but then crashed 60 miles from the airport. The investigation found the cause was controlled flight into terrain due to inadequate navigation under VFR conditions, inaccurate position reports, and failure to identify the airport.
probable_cause: The accident was caused by controlled flight into terrain due to inadequate navigation by the pilot whilst operating under VFR conditions; the pilot had sent inaccurate position reports and failed to identify the airport.

title: Eastern Air Lines 537
summary: On November 1, 1949, Eastern Air Lines Flight 537, a Douglas DC-4 on approach to Washington National Airport, collided in mid-air at 300 ft with a Lockheed P-38 Lightning being test-flown for the Bolivian Air Force, killing all 55 aboard the DC-4. The Civil Aeronautics Board found the P-38 pilot landed without proper clearance and failed to watch for conflicting traffic, while tower controllers also failed to warn Flight 537 of the developing traffic conflict in time.
probable_cause: The CAB found the primary causes were the P-38 pilot's decision to land without proper clearance and his failure to exercise normal vigilance for conflicting traffic; it also found tower controllers failed to notify Flight 537 earlier of the developing traffic situation, though this may not have changed the outcome.

events.text: The P-38 requested permission to land due to engine trouble and was cleared by the controller to join the left traffic pattern, but instead flew south and entered a long straight-in approach.

The P-38, considerably faster than the DC-4 on final, overtook Flight 537 a half mile southwest of the Runway 3 threshold.
The DC-4 was cut in half by the left propeller of the P-38 just forward of the trailing edge of the wing, killing all 55 aboard.

title: Hurum air disaster
summary: A Douglas DC-3 carrying 28 Jewish children from Tunisia to Israel, with seven escorts and crew, approached Oslo in heavy fog. The pilot lowered the aircraft in mountainous terrain while unable to see the ground, struck a tree with its wing, crashed into a mountain at 16:56, and caught fire. Of 35 people on board, 34 were killed including 27 children; only one 12-year-old boy survived.
probable_cause: The accident resulted from loss of situational awareness in instrument conditions; the pilot descended in mountainous terrain in heavy fog without being able to see the terrain and without adequate clearance from the ridges.

title: American Airlines 157
summary: American Airlines Flight 157, a Douglas DC-6, experienced failure of its No. 1 engine in mid-flight and continued toward Dallas Love Field. During approach with three engines, the aircraft experienced sudden airspeed loss and left wing drop at low altitude. The crew made critical errors while attempting recovery, resulting in loss of control, stall, and runway overrun. 28 fatalities resulted from the accident and fire.
